archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran bridge starter)
archetype.definition: A 14-year journeyman who wins by staying on schedule, taking what the scheme gives underneath and between the numbers, and not putting the ball in danger, rather than by pushing it downfield.

report.headline: Ben Johnson's under-center game made a 38-year-old backup efficient and turnover-free
report.take:
Keenum is what he has mostly been since 2013: a capable fill-in who runs the offense as called. The one full game in this dossier, a 27-7 home win over Philadelphia, fits that exactly. He went 24 of 34 for 247 yards with no interceptions and no sacks, at an intended air distance of 6.4 yards and a throw time of 2.41 seconds. He threw short and on time. The career line says this is his normal shape. His 2016 tracking showed a 2.38-second release, and his aggressiveness has sat between 16 and 23% every year it was charted. His only season with above-average efficiency was 2017 in Minnesota (+0.174 EPA per play, 11th). The other tracked years mostly ran near or below zero.

The structure around him drove the game. Under center he completed 13 of 14 for +0.818 EPA per play with an 86% success rate. Those are play-action and boot concepts built to defeat the defense before the throw. Out of shotgun he was 11 of 20 for -0.21 EPA per play. When he had to read it out from the gun, he was a below-average passer again. The seven intermediate throws (+0.912 EPA, two-thirds of his positive value) came largely from the same designs: middle-of-the-field windows created by motion and run action. A clean pocket helped too. He was pressured on just 8.8% of dropbacks, best among 32 charted passers, behind a line that ranks 4th in hit rate allowed.

The numbers hide two things. First, the 24.5 PPR points (3rd among 42) lean on a 1-yard designed-run touchdown. His four carries otherwise netted almost nothing, so his fantasy output overstates his passing. Second, the hard downs were shaky. On third down he was 3 of 8 with a -15.5 CPOE and a 37.5% conversion rate. The Bears also stopped throwing once ahead by nine or more, with five attempts at -0.581 EPA. He did put one ball on the ground (a turnover-worthy fumble), so the clean sheet was partly fortunate.

The dossier also has gaps. It lists Keenum as the Week 4 starter in a 23-12 win over the Jets, but that game isn't in his log or his totals. The depth chart also tags him QB3 as of October 5. Caleb Williams is out and week-to-week with an estimated October 18 return, so Keenum looks like the likeliest Week 5 starter. The depth-chart note means that shouldn't be treated as certain. Either way, this is a short bridge role, not a season.

strengths.title: Thrives inside play-action structure
strengths.body: He nearly perfected the under-center throws (92.9% completions, +25.4 CPOE), and that's where the scheme does the heavy lifting. As long as Johnson keeps calling it, the edge is repeatable, because it depends on the design more than on Keenum's arm. It is a 14-play sample, though.

strengths.title: Intermediate middle is the money zone
strengths.body: Seven throws in the 10-19 yard range produced +0.912 EPA each, and the middle of the field accounted for both passing touchdowns. These are timing throws to defined windows, which suits a veteran who sees the field quickly. The rate on seven attempts will come down, but the target area should keep producing.

strengths.title: Quick release protects the ball
strengths.body: A 2.41-second throw time and a clean pocket (8.8% pressured) produced zero sacks and zero picks. Getting the ball out has been his habit since 2016. The ball security is partly protection, which is now without a 65%-snap tackle in Braxton Jones.

concerns.title: Ordinary once the script runs out
concerns.body: Out of shotgun and on third down he was a below-average passer. On those plays he has to win with reads and accuracy rather than design. That isn't new: most of his tracked seasons since 2016 hovered near or below zero EPA. Expect the gap between scripted and unscripted plays to persist.

concerns.title: Fantasy line inflated by goal-line TD
concerns.body: Without the 1-yard designed-run score, his 24.5 PPR points would look more like a mid-tier passing day. His rushing EPA was -3.8 on four carries. A short-yardage touchdown can't be counted on each week.

concerns.title: Role is short-lived and unclear
concerns.body: Williams' estimated return is October 18, and the depth chart already lists Keenum as QB3. Even if he starts, this is likely a one- or two-game window. Any read beyond next week is mostly moot.

trend.note: Only the Week 3 Philadelphia game is in his log. It was efficient, conservative and clean, and it matches his career profile rather than signaling a change. The Week 4 Jets start isn't captured here.

nextGame.headline: Weak Packers pass defense, but it allows few explosive plays
nextGame.body:
Green Bay's defense ranks 27th in EPA and 25th against the pass. Its short-area defense is soft (19th), and that is exactly where Keenum lives. The catch is that the Packers allow the 4th-lowest explosive pass rate, and QBs have averaged only 220 yards against them (6th-fewest). This looks like a defense that bends underneath without breaking deep. That suits a 6.4-yard intended-air passer for efficiency, but it caps his yardage ceiling.

Availability tilts toward Chicago. Micah Parsons is out, and Edgerrin Cooper (83% of snaps) is lost for the year, which removes a key second-level defender against the intermediate middle Keenum attacked. CB Brandon Cisse (90% snaps) is questionable. Green Bay's offense is also missing C Jacob Monk and G Aaron Banks. That offense already ranks last in rushing EPA and 31st in hit rate allowed, and it now faces Chicago's 2nd-ranked pass defense and 4th-ranked sack rate. On Chicago's side, the loss of LT Braxton Jones is the one real threat to the clean pocket Keenum relied on.

keyMatchups.title: Keenum's middle vs Cooper-less linebackers
keyMatchups.body: His best throws came between the numbers at intermediate depth. Green Bay just lost an every-down linebacker for the season, which should open those windows behind run action. This is the clearest path to another efficient day.

keyMatchups.title: Bears defense vs battered GB offense
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's defense ranks 2nd against the pass, while Green Bay's offense is 25th in EPA, last in rushing and missing two interior linemen. If the Bears defense controls the game, Keenum gets the short fields and lead-protecting script that keep him in safe throws.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive ceiling is limited
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay rarely gives up big pass plays, and Keenum threw only two balls 20+ yards against Philadelphia. Drives will need to be long and patient, and that is where his third-down weakness can stall them.

nextGame.watch: How often Chicago lines him up under center: if the play-action share holds, he stays efficient, and if Green Bay forces him into shotgun on third-and-long, the offense stalls.

restOfSeason.body:
This is a bridge role. Williams is expected back around October 18, so Keenum's run is likely one more start, maybe two if the hamstring lingers. In that window, the scheme-driven efficiency is the sustainable part: play-action, quick throws and a strong line. The +0.213 EPA per dropback and 70.6% completion rate will likely drift toward his career norm of roughly average efficiency once opponents force more shotgun and third-down snaps. Rushing touchdowns and a zero-turnover rate shouldn't be projected forward; he already had one fumble.

For yardage, expect the same profile of 30-ish attempts at about 7 yards each, with little deep volume. Against defenses like Green Bay that limit explosives, the low end of that range is more likely.

bets.reason: Green Bay's offense ranks 25th in EPA and last in rushing, and it is missing its center and a guard against Chicago's 5th-ranked defense. Keenum's short, conservative passing meets a defense that allows the 4th-lowest explosive pass rate, so neither side projects to score fast.

The defensive mismatch strongly favors Chicago (2nd vs the pass, 4th in sack rate) against a banged-up Green Bay offense. The Packers are also without Parsons and Cooper on defense. It stays a lean because it's a road divisional game with a backup QB whose starting status the dossier leaves slightly unclear.

Quarterbacks have averaged 220 yards against Green Bay (6th-fewest), and the Packers rarely allow explosive passes. Keenum's 6.4-yard intended air distance leaves little room to beat that with big plays.
His 3rd-ranked PPR output rested on a 1-yard designed-run touchdown and an unusually efficient day under center. On four carries his rushing EPA was -3.8, so the scoring is unlikely to repeat.

confidence.note: One logged game, a missing Week 4 start, a QB3 depth-chart tag and a likely short window before Williams returns.
